idiom_name: frozen dataclass link record + urllib.parse.urljoin + http.client dereference
implementation_notes: Python has no URI type of its own, so the classic Link class collapses into a small @dataclass(frozen=True) Link carrying rel, href, and method/type metadata (dataclasses, PEP 557): frozen makes the link immutable and hashable, so it travels as an inert value inside dict payloads, queue items, or JSON across process boundaries. The producer builds relative hrefs and resolves them with urllib.parse.urljoin (RFC 3986 semantics); the consumer dereferences with http.client.HTTPConnection.request()/getresponse(), the low-level client urllib.request itself layers on. The stdlib ships no RFC 8288 Link-header parser, so relation metadata is carried inside the payload (a _links list of link objects) rather than the Link header. When a framework already emits hypermedia links (Django REST Framework, FastAPI response models), prefer its serializer-level link helpers and reserve the explicit dataclass form for message queues, webhooks, and plain-dict boundaries.
pitfalls: A mutable carrier (plain class or dict) is aliased wherever it travels: two components mutating the same Link object corrupt the 'link as inert value' invariant. Use @dataclass(frozen=True) so links stay immutable, hashable, and comparable as values.

urllib.parse.urljoin is documented as not secure with attacker-controlled input: an absolute href overrides the base and can send the dereference at an internal hostname (SSRF). Pin the expected base or allow-list the authority before following a link.
Never treat the presence of a link as an authorization grant: enforce authorization at dereference time, and sign or scope links that cross a trust boundary instead of trusting the href.

http.client.HTTPConnection is not thread-safe; following links concurrently over one shared connection corrupts the wire protocol. Give each consumer thread its own connection or mediate access through a pool.

Python has no ownership transfer: the producer's runtime still owns the referenced resource, and a deleted target turns every in-flight link into a 404 (a dangling reference, not a crash). Keep lifetime with the producer and back hrefs with a registry or redirect layer.
